scenario_text: A regional water utility has established a utilities dynamic market for routine maintenance works and has already published a qualifying dynamic market notice to advertise it. The utility now wants to award a specific maintenance contract to suppliers who are already members of that market rather than running a fresh open competition. The procurement officer is unsure whether the usual public tender notice route still has to be followed, or whether a different notification process applies because the suppliers are already inside an established market.
query: We've set up a utilities dynamic market for our maintenance work and want to award a contract to companies already inside it. Do we still need to publish a normal public tender notice for this award, or does a different process apply to notifying the market members?

evidence_requirements.description: The general duty to publish a tender notice before inviting suppliers under an open procedure or competitive flexible procedure

The specific exception disapplying the section 21 tender notice duty for awards by reference to membership of a utilities dynamic market, and the replacement duty to provide (rather than publish) a tender notice to market members

notes: Combines tender_notices with the utilities dynamic market provisions; exact anchor is s.40's replacement of the s.21 duty.

scenario_text: A district council's commercial team is planning a facilities management contract with an estimated whole-life value of around £195,000, excluding VAT. The council is a sub-central (i.e. not central government) contracting authority. The team needs to establish whether this value brings the contract within the full procurement regime as a regulated public contract, or whether it falls under the below-threshold rules instead, since that determines which set of publication duties apply from the outset.
query: We're about to run a facilities management procurement worth around £195,000 for the council. How do we work out whether this contract has to go through the full procurement process, or whether it counts as below the relevant threshold for a body like ours?

evidence_requirements.description: That a contract is only a regulated 'public contract' if its estimated value is not less than the threshold amount for that type of contract
The specific threshold amount applicable to a contract for goods, services or works awarded by a sub-central government authority (as opposed to central government)

notes: Exact anchor is the £207,720 sub-central threshold figure in Schedule 1 para 1 row 12, read together with the s.3 threshold-based definition of 'public contract'.

scenario_text: A central government department has completed a competitive tendering procedure for a services contract and has decided on a winning bidder. The contract manager wants to sign the contract as quickly as possible, but a losing bidder has already hinted it may challenge the outcome. The contract manager needs to know exactly how long the department must wait after notifying the market of the award decision before the contract can actually be signed.
query: We've decided who's won our tender and want to sign the contract quickly, but a losing bidder is unhappy. How long do we legally have to wait after telling the market about the award decision before we can actually sign the contract?

evidence_requirements.description: The length of the mandatory standstill period and the event that starts it running

notes: Single clean anchor: s.51 mandatory standstill period of 8 working days beginning with publication of the contract award notice.

scenario_text: An NHS trust is evaluating a bidder for a facilities contract. The trust's own records show that this supplier significantly underperformed on a previous contract with a different NHS body, was given a proper opportunity to improve, and still failed to meet the required standard. Legal advice is being sought both on whether the trust can act on this history in the current competition and on whether the matter could be escalated so that the supplier is considered for a government-wide debarment listing.
query: One of our bidders has a documented history of failing to meet contract standards for another NHS body, even after being given a chance to improve. Can we take that into account when deciding whether this supplier can compete for our contract, and separately, is there a route for that kind of track record to lead to the supplier being barred from public contracts more broadly?

evidence_requirements.description: Whether a supplier's history of poor performance on a previous contract, after being given a chance to improve, can make it an 'excludable supplier' in the trust's own procurement
The separate, centrally-managed route by which an appropriate authority can investigate a supplier and add it to the government-wide debarment list

notes: Deliberately tests the distinction between contracting-authority-level discretionary exclusion (s.57(2) + Sch.7 para 12) and centrally-run debarment (s.60/s.62), which are easy to conflate.

scenario_text: A central government department's commercial policy team wants to alert the market to a major upcoming IT procurement several months before the formal tender process begins, so that suppliers have time to prepare and mobilise resources. The team is checking whether publishing this kind of early notice is a legal requirement or a voluntary option, and what information it would need to contain if they choose to publish one.
query: We want to alert the market early about a big IT procurement that's still months away from going out to tender, so suppliers have time to prepare. Is publishing that kind of early notice something we're required to do, and what would we need to include in it?

evidence_requirements.description: That a planned procurement notice is optional (not mandatory) and may be published before a tender notice, including the timing window for it to count as a 'qualifying' notice
The specific information that regulations require a planned procurement notice to contain

notes: Cross-instrument anchor: the enabling power and voluntary nature sit in PA2023 s.15, while the detailed content requirements sit in Procurement Regulations 2024 reg.16.

scenario_text: A council ran a full open competition for a school catering contract. Only one tender was received, and on evaluation it materially failed the specification and would have been disregarded under the authority's own published assessment methodology. The incumbent contract expires in six weeks and there is no time to re-run the full competition.
query: We published a full tender competition for this contract but the only response we got doesn't meet our requirements and would fail evaluation anyway. Can we just go and agree a contract with a supplier we already trust instead of running the competition again, and is there anything we have to publish first if we do that?

evidence_requirements.description: Whether a direct award to a supplier is permitted where a competitive tendering procedure produced no suitable tender/request
What notice must be published before making such a direct award

scenario_text: An NHS trust is procuring a routine medical consumables contract under budget pressure. The finance lead wants to skip any quality or service scoring entirely and award purely to whichever compliant bidder quotes the lowest total price.
query: Is it actually allowed for us to score bids purely on price and ignore quality altogether, or do we always have to build in some kind of non-price scoring criteria?

evidence_requirements.description: Whether price/cost alone may be the sole award criterion for identifying the most advantageous tender
What wider duties must still be considered before choosing price as the sole criterion

scenario_text: A central government department is finalising a tender pack for a services contract. The legal team has asked bid teams to require that (a) bidders already have contract-specific insurance in place before the contract is signed, and (b) every bidder, including very small suppliers, submit three years of audited financial statements.
query: Before we finalise the tender pack, can we insist bidders already have the contract-specific insurance in place before we award, and can we require audited accounts from every single bidder, even the very small ones?

evidence_requirements.description: Whether a condition of participation may require insurance to be in place before contract award
Whether a condition of participation may require audited accounts from suppliers not otherwise legally required to have them audited

scenario_text: A water utility wants to set up a framework for a major capital works programme expected to run for around ten years, given the scale of infrastructure investment and the time suppliers need to recoup mobilisation costs.
query: Our capital programme arrangement needs to run well beyond the usual term cap on these agreements - is there a route that lets us keep something like this going for a decade, and if so what does setting it up that way actually require us to build in from the start?

evidence_requirements.description: The standard maximum term for a framework and the conditions for exceeding it
Whether an open framework scheme is exempt from the standard term cap and what structure it must follow instead

notes: Touches both frameworks and open_frameworks topics; combination flagged per instructions.

scenario_text: A council has been running a qualified-supplier list for temporary agency staff for eighteen months. To cut administrative overhead, the category manager wants to stop assessing new supplier applications for the rest of the arrangement's life and just keep working with the suppliers already on the list.
query: Once we've got a solid working group of suppliers on our staffing list, can we just close it to new joiners for a while to cut down on admin, or are we required to keep taking new applications the whole time the arrangement runs?

evidence_requirements.description: Whether a contracting authority must continue accepting and assessing new membership applications throughout the life of a dynamic market

scenario_text: A university is scoping a five-year estates maintenance contract worth several million pounds. It has always been let as one large single contract to one national provider, but the sustainability team has raised concerns that this locks out smaller regional and specialist contractors from ever bidding.
query: Before we go out to market on this one, do we actually have to stop and think about splitting it into smaller packages to give smaller firms a chance, or can we just carry on letting it as one big contract like we always have?

evidence_requirements.description: Whether there is a duty to consider dividing a contract into lots before publishing a tender notice
How the duty to have regard to barriers facing SMEs relates to the lots decision

notes: Touches both lots and procurement_objectives topics; combination flagged per instructions.

scenario_text: A government department is about to sign a seven-million-pound contract for high-level strategic policy advisory services, where outputs are largely qualitative and evolve throughout the engagement.
query: This contract is well above the usual reporting threshold - are we legally required to set specific measurable performance indicators for it no matter what, or is there any get-out if the kind of work just doesn't lend itself to that kind of scoring?

evidence_requirements.description: The mandatory duty to set at least three KPIs on contracts above the value threshold
The exemption where a supplier's performance could not appropriately be assessed by reference to KPIs

scenario_text: We are running a competition for a highways maintenance contract. One of the bidders performed very badly on a waste-collection contract for a neighbouring council two years ago, with persistent late running and defects the council had to fix itself. Nobody ever took the bidder to court over it, and there was no formal finding against them. We are trying to work out whether we are even allowed to hold that history against them at the shortlisting stage.
query: A bidder has a well-documented history of seriously underperforming on a previous public contract, even though nobody sued them over it or got a court ruling. Are we allowed to factor that track record into whether they can take part in our competition, and if so, what do we need to be able to show?

evidence_requirements.description: Serious, sufficiently-severe breach of a previous public contract (whether or not there was a court ruling) can itself be a ground allowing the authority to treat the supplier as excludable.

To rely on that ground the authority must be applying the 'excludable supplier' test, which requires considering whether the circumstances are continuing or likely to recur, subject to the general 5-year lookback limit on discretionary grounds.

scenario_text: We're about to award a large IT services contract centrally. Before signing, one of the team asked whether there is a central register we're obliged to check to rule out bidders who have effectively been shut out of public sector work government-wide, as opposed to being excluded only from our own specific competition.
query: Is there a government-wide list of suppliers who are barred from all public contracts, and are we required to check it before we sign, or does exclusion only ever operate competition-by-competition?

evidence_requirements.description: A supplier or associated person appearing on the centrally-kept debarment list is, by that fact alone, an excluded or excludable supplier for any contracting authority, distinct from an authority's own case-by-case exclusion determination.
The debarment list is created and maintained through a Minister-led investigation and entry process, with practical guidance on when and how it becomes relevant during procurement.

scenario_text: Six months into a facilities management contract, we discovered that the contractor's parent company was convicted of a serious fraud offence shortly after we signed. Nothing like this was known to us, or discoverable, at the time of contract award. Some colleagues want to let the contract keep running since day-to-day service is fine; others think we have to act because of what's come to light.
query: If a supplier becomes caught up in something that would normally have kept them out of the running, but this only comes to light after the contract has already started, can we pull the plug on the deal now, and what do we have to do before and after we do?

evidence_requirements.description: It is an implied term of every public contract that it can be terminated where the supplier has, since award, become an excluded or excludable supplier; before terminating, the authority must notify the supplier, specify the ground, and give a reasonable opportunity to make representations.
Once a public contract is terminated, the authority must publish a contract termination notice within 30 days of termination.

scenario_text: Our estates team has a five-year grounds-maintenance contract with a single supplier. Fuel and wage costs have risen in ways nobody could reasonably have predicted when the original competition was run, and the supplier says it cannot keep delivering at the agreed price. We would rather adjust the price with the existing supplier than start a brand-new competition from scratch.
query: If costs on a live contract rise for reasons nobody could have seen coming, how far can we adjust the price with our existing supplier before that change becomes big enough that we would be required to go back out to competition instead?

evidence_requirements.description: A price change driven by circumstances that could not reasonably have been foreseen before award is a permitted modification, provided it does not change the overall nature of the contract and (for a non-utilities contract) does not increase the estimated contract value by more than 50 per cent.

More generally, a modification counts as 'substantial' (and is not permitted without a new procurement) if, among other things, it changes the contract term by more than 10 per cent, or materially changes scope or the economic balance in the supplier's favour.

scenario_text: We've identified our preferred bidder for a new energy-metering framework and want to move quickly to signature. Someone in finance mentioned there might be a mandatory pause we have to observe before we can actually commit to the contract.
query: Once we've picked a winning bidder, is there a mandatory waiting period we must observe before we can sign the contract, how long is it, and are there any situations where we can go straight to signature without waiting?

evidence_requirements.description: A contracting authority may not enter into the public contract before the end of the mandatory standstill period, which is 8 working days beginning with the day the contract award notice is published.

The mandatory standstill period does not apply to certain contracts (e.g. direct awards for extreme and unavoidable urgency or to protect life, private-utility direct awards, framework call-offs, dynamic market awards, light touch contracts) though a voluntary standstill period of at least 8 working days may still be provided for.

scenario_text: We ran an open competitive tendering procedure for a highways resurfacing contract. Only one tender was submitted, and it was disregarded because the supplier failed to meet a mandatory technical requirement, so in practice we received no suitable tender at all. Senior management wants to move quickly and place the contract directly with a contractor we already trust, rather than re-running the whole procedure.
query: Can we switch straight to a direct award with a supplier of our choosing after a competitive procedure produced no suitable tenders, and if so what do we need to check or publish before we go ahead?

evidence_requirements.description: Legal basis permitting a contracting authority to switch to direct award where a competitive tendering procedure produced no suitable tenders or requests to participate
Separate transparency obligation: a transparency notice must be published before awarding under this route, distinct from the substantive power to switch

notes: Distinct from TEST011: this turns on failed competition (s.43)/transparency (s.44); TEST011 turns on urgency (Sch5 para13)/standstill exemption (s.51(3)(a)).

scenario_text: An NHS trust has an existing facilities management contract. Six months into the term, an additional building has come into use earlier than planned, and the trust wants to add that building to the scope of the existing contract rather than tendering separately. The change would increase the contract's value by roughly 12 per cent.
query: Are we allowed to add this extra building to the existing contract without starting a fresh procurement, and is there anything we have to publish before we make the change?

evidence_requirements.description: Grounds on which a public contract may be modified without a new procurement procedure
Separate pre-modification transparency duty to publish a contract change notice, subject to its own value/term thresholds

notes: Distinct from TEST012 (automatic suspension during modification standstill).

scenario_text: A university group is setting up a new framework for IT hardware and managed services. Because of long technology refresh and integration cycles, the commercial team wants the framework to run for six years, longer than they believe is normally allowed.
query: Is there a hard cap on how long a new framework can run, and if we want to go beyond the usual limit because of the nature of what we're buying, is there anything specific we need to record or publish?

evidence_requirements.description: The statutory cap on framework term (four years generally, eight years for defence/security or utilities frameworks) and the exception allowing a longer term where the nature of the goods/services requires it
Separate duty triggered by relying on the longer-term exception: reasons must be set out in the tender or transparency notice for the framework

scenario_text: A government department is designing a novel digital case-management system and wants to speak informally with a small number of specialist suppliers before going out to tender, to understand what is technically feasible and refine the specification.
query: Are we allowed to talk to suppliers like this before we go out to tender, what do we need to do to keep it fair to everyone, and is there anything we need to publish about it?

evidence_requirements.description: Power to carry out preliminary market engagement and the fairness safeguard duty (must avoid unfair advantage/distortion of competition, with exclusion as the consequence if an advantage cannot be avoided)
Separate transparency duty to publish a preliminary market engagement notice before the tender notice, or explain in the tender notice why one was not published

scenario_text: A council's finance team has just gone live with a new invoicing system for a large multi-year highways maintenance contract, and contract managers want to understand their statutory obligations around paying the contractor's invoices.
query: Is there a legal deadline by which we must pay this supplier's invoices, and do we have any separate obligation to report on how well we're paying on time?

evidence_requirements.description: Implied 30-day payment term in every public contract (subject to limited exceptions)
Separate biannual reporting duty: a payments compliance notice must be published regardless of individual invoice disputes, covering payment performance over each reporting period

scenario_text: A council needs several batches of similar specialist furniture for different sites over the coming year. Each individual order would come in comfortably under the council's procurement threshold, and a colleague has suggested placing them as separate below-threshold purchases to avoid running a full tender.
query: Can we deliberately structure these as separate smaller purchases to stay under the threshold, and if we do have a genuinely below-threshold contract, what do we still need to publish?

evidence_requirements.description: Anti-avoidance valuation rule: contracts that could reasonably be supplied as a single contract must generally have their values aggregated, and a contracting authority must not exercise discretion in valuing a contract with a view to avoiding a requirement of the Act
Separate publication duties that apply to a genuinely below-threshold contract: a below-threshold tender notice before advertising, and a contract details notice after entering into the contract

scenario_text: A council is planning a regional grounds-maintenance procurement covering several district areas. The commercial team is deciding whether to run it as one large contract or split it geographically, and is also wary of a single contractor winning every area and becoming a point of failure.
query: Do we actually have to consider splitting this into separate area-based contracts, and if we do go with separate lots, can we limit how many a single bidder is allowed to win?

evidence_requirements.description: Duty to consider, before publishing a tender notice, whether the requirement could reasonably be supplied under more than one contract and awarded by lots, and to lot the award or give reasons for not doing so
Separate rule permitting a cap on the number of lots awarded to any one supplier, subject to providing an objective mechanism for supplier selection where the cap would otherwise be exceeded

scenario_text: Corrigan Vale District Council awarded a five-year highways resurfacing and maintenance contract in January 2025 following a competitive tender run entirely under the Public Contracts Regulations 2015. The Procurement Act 2023 has since come fully into force. The council's commercial team now wants to instruct additional resurfacing works using a price-revision options clause that was included in the original tender documents, and needs to know which set of rules currently governs any change to this specific contract.
query: We ran our competition and awarded this contract under the old procurement regulations, just before the new Procurement Act rules came into force. We now want to use an options clause from our original tender documents to instruct some extra resurfacing works. Does a live contract like this automatically move onto the new Act's rules for making changes now that the Act is in force, or does something else determine which rulebook we follow?

evidence_requirements.description: Identify which legal regime governs the modification of a contract that was awarded under the Public Contracts Regulations 2015 before the Procurement Act 2023 commenced, given that the Act is now fully in force.
Identify the specific PCR2015 rule that permits modification via a review/options clause included in the original procurement documents without a new procurement procedure.

notes: Shares reg 5 transitional-saving mechanism with TEST013, different substantive question (modification rules vs termination right).

scenario_text: A central government department wants to commission a short piece of research from a specialist consultancy at an estimated value of about £18,000, without running a full competitive tender. Some colleagues in the department have suggested that because the contract's value is well below the international-agreement procurement thresholds, none of the Procurement Act 2023's rules need to be complied with at all before the department goes ahead.
query: We're about to award a contract worth roughly £18,000 to a consultancy without running a full competition, since it's a small piece of work that's well below the usual procurement threshold. Before we go ahead, do we still have any publication or notice duties under the Procurement Act, or does the Act simply not apply once you're below the main threshold figure?

evidence_requirements.description: Determine whether a below-threshold contract of this value still triggers publication obligations under the Procurement Act 2023, and identify the relevant minimum value and notice requirements (the 'notifiable below-threshold contract' concept).
Confirm that the contracting authority must estimate the contract's value in accordance with the Act's valuation rules and must not manipulate that estimate with a view to avoiding requirements.

notes: Related in subject to TEST015 but asks a different question (whether any obligations attach at all vs whether modification rules apply to an existing below-threshold contract).

scenario_text: A university set up a four-year framework for temporary academic and administrative staffing three years ago. It was not established as part of a rolling 'open framework' scheme, and it is not a defence, security or utilities framework. With the framework due to expire soon, the university's category manager would like to simply extend it for a further two years rather than running a fresh competition, since re-tendering mid-academic-year would be disruptive.
query: We have a staffing framework that's coming up to its expiry date, and we'd like to just extend it for another couple of years rather than re-running the whole competition, since it's working well operationally. Is there a hard statutory limit on how long a framework like this can run, or can we extend it by agreement if both sides are willing?

evidence_requirements.description: Identify the statutory maximum term for an ordinary (non-defence/security, non-utilities) framework under the Procurement Act 2023, and whether that limit can be extended by agreement of the parties.

Confirm that the only statutory route to a longer overall lifespan (an open framework scheme of successive frameworks) is not available here because it must be structured as an open framework from the outset.

scenario_text: An NHS trust holds a multi-supplier facilities management framework. It has just run a mini-competition among the framework suppliers and wants to place a call-off contract with the winning supplier. Contract managers at the trust are used to observing a mandatory pre-contract standstill period whenever they award contracts following a full open competition and assume the same rule must apply here.
query: We're about to award a call-off contract to one of our framework suppliers after running a mini-competition between them. Do we have to observe the same mandatory standstill period before we sign that we would for a contract awarded through a full open tender, or does the position differ for call-off contracts under a framework?

evidence_requirements.description: Determine whether the Procurement Act 2023's mandatory standstill period applies to a contract awarded in accordance with a framework (a call-off contract).
Note that although the mandatory standstill does not apply to call-off contracts, a voluntary standstill period can still be provided for in the contract award notice.

scenario_text: A local authority is midway through evaluating tenders in a live procurement. One bidder marked its pricing schedule and technical method statement as commercially confidential when it submitted its tender. Before the contract is awarded, the authority receives a Freedom of Information request from a local journalist asking for full copies of all tenders received, including pricing.
query: We've had an FOI request asking for full copies of the tenders in an ongoing procurement, including a bidder's pricing, which they've told us is commercially sensitive. Can we withhold that information, and what would we need to be able to show if the requester or the bidder challenged our decision?

evidence_requirements.description: Identify the Procurement Act 2023 basis on which a contracting authority may withhold sensitive commercial information from disclosure, and what it must still do if it withholds information.

Identify the Freedom of Information Act 2000 exemption governing an actual FOI request for commercial/tender information, that it is a qualified exemption subject to a public interest balance, and how the regulator applies that balance to procurement information specifically.

scenario_text: Our authority is about to award a £6.2 million grounds maintenance and winter gritting contract to a single supplier. This is our first contract over the £5 million threshold since the new procurement regime came into force, and our contract management team has not previously had to run a formal KPI regime linked to statutory notices. We need to build the ongoing monitoring and reporting cycle into our contract management plan before the contract starts.
query: We're about to enter into a £6.2 million grounds maintenance contract. What should our ongoing key performance indicator process look like once the contract is live -- how many KPIs do we need, and how often do we need to assess and publish performance against them?

evidence_requirements.description: Identify the duty to set at least three KPIs for contracts over £5m and how/where they must be published (via the contract, and the contract details notice).
Identify the ongoing duty to assess supplier performance against the KPIs at least once every 12 months and on termination, and publish the results via a contract performance notice.

scenario_text: A central government department runs several multi-year facilities and IT support contracts, each with layers of sub-contractors. Following recent changes to the procurement rules, the finance and commercial teams have been asked to jointly design a payment monitoring process that will let the department demonstrate compliance without waiting for an external audit to flag problems. No such process currently exists across the department's contract portfolio.
query: We want to set up an internal process for monitoring and reporting on payment performance across our contracts and their supply chains. What information do we need to track, and how often do we need to publish it, to stay compliant?

evidence_requirements.description: Identify the six-monthly payments compliance notice obligation tied to the implied 30-day payment term (and its extension to sub-contracts).
Identify the separate quarterly duty to publish specified information about individual payments over £30,000 made under a public contract.

scenario_text: An NHS trust is planning to replace its diagnostic imaging service ahead of a major tender, and wants to talk to manufacturers and service providers early to understand what solutions are realistically available before finalising its specification. The category manager is conscious that the trust has an existing supplier for related equipment and does not want the process to be seen as tailoring the eventual competition around that supplier.
query: We want to talk to potential suppliers before we go out to tender, to understand what's available and help us write a realistic specification, but we're worried this could be seen as favouring our existing supplier or distorting the eventual competition. What do we actually need to do to run this safely?

evidence_requirements.description: Identify the practical steps to avoid giving a participating supplier an unfair advantage or distorting competition during preliminary market engagement, including the consequence if an unavoidable advantage arises.
Identify the requirement to publish a preliminary market engagement notice before the tender notice, or to explain in the tender notice why one was not published.

scenario_text: A university is preparing to re-tender its combined grounds maintenance and cleaning services across several campuses in different towns. Historically this has been awarded as one large contract to a single national provider, but the estates team wants to know whether the rules now require them to think about dividing the requirement into separate lots, and what they need to do if they decide to keep it as one contract.
query: Before we go out to tender for our combined estates services contract across several campuses, do we need to consider splitting the requirement into lots, and what do we need to record if we decide to keep it as a single contract?

evidence_requirements.description: Identify the duty to consider whether the requirement could reasonably be split into lots before publishing a tender notice, and the duty to record/give reasons if choosing not to.
Identify practical operational options once lots are used, e.g. limiting the number of lots any one supplier can be awarded, and what must be published per lot.

scenario_text: A council frequently procures small, similar-value repairs and minor works packages throughout the year and wants to stop running a full tender exercise each time. It is considering establishing a standing pool of qualified suppliers it can call off from as work arises, and wants to understand practically how such a pool is set up and kept compliant, including what happens if a supplier on the list later becomes subject to an exclusion ground.
query: We're considering setting up a rolling pool of pre-qualified suppliers for repeat minor works, rather than re-tendering every time. What's the practical process for establishing this and keeping the supplier list compliant over time, including what we need to do if a supplier on the list later becomes an excluded supplier?

evidence_requirements.description: Identify the establishment process and notice stages for setting up a dynamic market.
Identify the duty (and discretion) to remove a supplier from a dynamic market once it becomes an excluded/excludable supplier, and the process for doing so.

scenario_text: A central government department's commercial team has just been told by the Cabinet Office that one of its suppliers has been entered onto the published debarment list following an investigation. The supplier has written to the department stating that it intends to challenge the decision, and a commercial colleague has already told the department's legal adviser (based on a law firm blog post) that the supplier can simply ask the Minister informally to reconsider. Before replying to the supplier's letter, the legal adviser wants to check what the actual legal mechanism for challenging a debarment listing is, including any time limits and what a court can and cannot do.
query: Is there an actual statutory route for a supplier to challenge being placed on the debarment list, with a defined time limit and remedy, or is that just something people describe informally? I need the real legal mechanism here, not a summary from a blog.

evidence_requirements.description: Identify the binding statutory mechanism(s) by which a supplier can challenge or suspend the effect of a debarment list entry, including who can bring proceedings, the grounds, the time limit, and what remedy a court can grant.

notes: Seed lead also surfaced UKSI 2025 163 reg 20D (the Minister's power to investigate for debarment purposes) - verified as real but it governs the investigation stage, not how a supplier challenges the resulting listing, so it was not used as evidence for this scenario.

scenario_text: A local authority's commercial manager has received a Freedom of Information request from a local journalist asking for the full pricing breakdown submitted by the winning bidder in a recently awarded contract. The winning supplier has objected, saying the figures were marked confidential in its tender and should not be released. A colleague has told the commercial manager that marking something 'confidential' in a tender automatically means it can be withheld, but the commercial manager is not convinced that is actually how the law works.
query: We've had an FOI request for a supplier's pricing information from a contract we just awarded, and the supplier says it's commercially sensitive. Is there an actual legal exemption that lets us withhold it, and what's the real test that applies, not just what the supplier assumes because they marked it confidential?

evidence_requirements.description: Identify the binding legal exemption and test that governs whether commercially sensitive tender/pricing information can lawfully be withheld from an FOI requester (not merely that the supplier labelled it confidential).

notes: Two seed leads were rejected as noise after verification: 'UKPGA 2025 36' (an unrelated Act about employer/work-finding-agency disclosure duties) and Freedom of Information Act 2000 s.27 (international-relations exemption, wrong legal issue). The actually on-point FOIA provision is s.43 (commercial interests), confirmed independently.

scenario_text: A procurement officer at a university is running a multi-stage competitive procedure and is about to let bidders progress to the next stage. A colleague mentioned that checking whether a bidder has a history of past misconduct that could affect its standing is 'best practice' but not something the university is legally obliged to do unless the bidder already appears on the published debarment list. The procurement officer wants to check whether that is actually correct before letting anyone through to the next stage.
query: Before we let a bidder move on to the next stage of our procurement, is there an actual legal requirement to check whether they should be excluded, or is that just recommended good practice? I want to know what the law itself requires, not a training summary.

evidence_requirements.description: Identify the binding statutory duty requiring a contracting authority to determine whether a supplier is an excluded or excludable supplier before permitting it to participate further in a competitive flexible procedure, and confirm what that determination legally requires the authority to do with each category.

notes: UKSI 2025 163 reg 20D (debarment-list investigations) is a different mechanism from the s.27/s.57 pre-participation check, so it was not reused here.

scenario_text: A county council's highways team invited tenders for a term maintenance contract through an open competitive tendering procedure. All of the tenders received were rejected as technically non-compliant with the specification, and no compliant bids remain in play. The team is under time pressure to get a contractor mobilised before winter gritting season and is considering placing the contract directly with one of the bidders that submitted a rejected tender, rather than re-running the competition. Nobody on the team has pinned down exactly when, in procurement-process terms, the original tendering exercise is treated as having started, which matters given the recent change in the procurement rules.
query: We invited tenders for a highways contract but every bid we got back was rejected as unsuitable. Can we now just award the contract directly to one of those bidders without starting a new competition, and what do we need to check or publish before doing that?

evidence_requirements.description: Identify the specific statutory mechanism that permits switching from a competitive tendering procedure to direct award of the same contract after receiving no suitable tenders, under both the current regime and the regime it replaced, since which one governs this procurement is not established by the facts given.

Identify the transitional/saving rule that determines whether this procurement is still governed by the Public Contracts Regulations 2015 or by the Procurement Act 2023, and flag that the query does not supply the fact (the date/step at which the tendering procedure commenced) needed to resolve this.

Identify the notice(s) that must be published before the direct award can be made under whichever regime applies (a transparency notice under the Act, or the equivalent contract award notice step under the 2015 Regulations), since the officer explicitly asked what must be checked/published first.

notes: Compound: combines switch_competition_to_direct_award with applicability_transitional. Deliberately omits the fact determining which regime applies.

scenario_text: An NHS trust's commercial team put in place a multi-supplier framework for clinical equipment maintenance a few years ago. One of the suppliers on the framework has asked for an 18-month extension to its individual call-off contract because of ongoing supply-chain disruption affecting spare parts. Separately, the trust is approaching the point where it would otherwise need to re-run the framework competition, and someone has suggested simply rolling the existing framework forward instead of starting a fresh procurement. Nobody has flagged whether the framework was set up before or after the most recent change in procurement legislation.
query: One of our framework suppliers wants an 18-month extension on their call-off contract because of supply problems, and separately we're wondering whether we can just extend the framework itself rather than re-competing it when it reaches its original end date. Are either of those changes allowed without a new procurement, and how far could we realistically go?

evidence_requirements.description: Distinguish between extending an individual call-off contract awarded under the framework (governed by general contract-modification rules) and extending the framework agreement itself (governed by framework-specific maximum-term rules), since the query conflates the two.
Identify the applicable modification test and numeric limits for extending the call-off contract's term under whichever regime governs this framework.

Identify the maximum permitted term for the framework itself and the narrow circumstances in which it can exceed the default cap, under whichever regime governs, since the query doesn't establish when the framework was set up.

notes: Compound: combines frameworks with contract_modification, omits framework establishment date.

scenario_text: A central government department has a services contract where the supplier has repeatedly missed the performance targets set out at the start of the contract, despite being told about it and given time to put things right. The department's contract manager wants to terminate but isn't sure whether repeated poor performance against the targets is, by itself, a lawful ground for termination, or whether anything needs to be formally reported or published about the poor performance regardless of what is decided about the contract itself. The contract's own termination clauses haven't yet been reviewed by legal, and the contract's value and exact award date haven't been confirmed.
query: A supplier on one of our contracts keeps missing the performance targets we set, even after we've raised it with them and given them a chance to sort it out. Can we terminate for that on its own, and separately, do we have any obligation to report or publish anything about the poor performance?

evidence_requirements.description: Determine whether persistent poor performance against agreed targets is, by itself, one of the specific statutory termination grounds, as opposed to depending on the contract's own express or implied termination terms, under whichever regime governs this contract.
Identify the specific statutory duty to publish information about a supplier's poor performance / failure to improve, which applies independently of whether the contract is actually terminated.

Flag that whether the KPI-setting and performance-publication duties apply at all depends on facts not given in the query -- the contract's value and which regime governs, since the predecessor regime has no direct equivalent duty.

notes: Compound: combines termination with kpis_performance. Query assumes poor performance is itself a termination trigger; corpus shows statutory grounds are narrower.
